messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 52
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Maid
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 51

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Ravi is a 52-year-old South Asian man who works as a maid for a residential cleaning company in a midsized Midwestern city. He came to therapy reluctantly, referred by his primary care doctor after a routine checkup revealed elevated blood pressure and a tremor in his hands that had been getting worse over the past year. When the doctor asked about stress, Ravi sat silently for a long moment, then said, "I don't sleep. I don't feel like myself. I don't feel like anything." He agreed to come only after the doctor told him his heart was showing signs of strain.

The event that changed everything happened eighteen months ago. Ravi had been cleaning a fifth-floor apartment alone on a Tuesday afternoon. He was vacuuming the living room when he noticed the client's elderly cat sleeping under the sofa. He finished the room, moved to the bedroom, and when he returned to the living room to gather his supplies, he saw that the cat had crawled into the vacuum cleaner bag he had left open on the floor. The cat was dead. Ravi remembers the moment as a series of still images: the cat's body, the open bag, his own hands frozen on the vacuum handle. He remembers the sound that came out of him, a kind of choked cry. He remembers calling his supervisor, who told him to leave the apartment and come back to the office. He remembers the client calling him later that evening, weeping, asking how this could have happened. He had no answer.

What haunts Ravi most is not the image of the cat itself, though that comes back to him without warning. He can be pushing a cart down a hotel hallway, or standing at a red light, or reaching for a cup of water in his own kitchen, and suddenly he is back in that apartment, the vacuum in his hands, the weight of what he has done pressing down on him. The rage that floods him in those moments is enormous, and it is directed entirely at himself. He has come to believe that he acted carelessly, that he was rushing, that he failed to check the room properly because he was thinking about his next job instead of paying attention to what mattered. He tells himself that a good person would have looked. A careful person would have seen the cat. The fact that he did not means something about who he is.

Since that Tuesday, Ravi has stopped feeling that his life has any direction. He goes to work because he has to pay rent, but he no longer takes pride in his work. He used to enjoy making a space clean and orderly; now he simply moves through the motions, his mind elsewhere. He has stopped calling his adult daughter, who lives in another state, because he does not know what to say to her. He is certain that if she knew what he had done, she would see him differently. He has stopped going to the temple, where he used to attend weekly services. He tells himself he has no right to be there, that he acted in a way that goes against everything he was taught about kindness and care toward living things.

The worst part, Ravi says, is that the memory comes back without any warning. He can be fine, and then something in his surroundings—the sound of a vacuum in another unit, the sight of a cat on a windowsill, the smell of a particular cleaning solution—and he is back in that apartment, the rage and shame and disbelief washing over him all at once. His hands start to shake. His chest tightens. He has learned to excuse himself to the supply closet until it passes. His supervisor has noticed that he takes longer on his routes than he used to. Ravi has told her he is just being more thorough. In truth, he is avoiding certain apartments. He has asked not to be scheduled in buildings that allow pets. He has started taking the stairs instead of the elevator because the enclosed space makes him feel trapped when a memory hits. His social world has shrunk to almost nothing. He eats alone, watches television without really seeing it, and waits for the next wave to come.

What finally brought Ravi to seek help was not the intrusive memories or the rage or the loss of meaning, though all of those had been present for months. It was the moment last week when he was cleaning a bathroom and caught a glimpse of himself in the mirror. He did not recognize the person looking back. He thought, "I am not a person anymore. I am just what happened." That thought frightened him in a way the others had not. He is not sure therapy can help. He is not sure he deserves to feel better. But he came, and he sat down, and he told the story. He is afraid that if he talks about it, he will only confirm what he already believes: that he is someone who did something unforgivable. He is also afraid, somewhere underneath that, of staying like this forever.
